## What this session covers

The rest of the workshop assumes you know what these tools actually are, so this is the
hour that puts that in place. What a large language model does mechanically, why that
explains both what it's good at and how it fails, and which of the things people commonly
believe about them are wrong.

You don't need a technical background for any of this. The goal is that by the end of the
hour you can predict, before you try it, whether a given classroom task is one these tools
will handle well.

## Session outline

| Time | Segment |
|-----:|:--------|
| ~15 min | What a language model actually does |
| ~25 min | Where it's strong, where it fails, and why those are the same fact |
| ~20 min | Common misconceptions, and questions |

## Key points

- A language model predicts likely next words. Everything it does well and everything it
  gets wrong follows from that one fact.
- Fluency and accuracy are separate properties. Confident, well-formed, and wrong is the
  normal failure, not an unusual one.
- The reliable rule of thumb: these tools are strong when you supply the content and ask
  them to change its form, and weak when you ask them to supply the content.
- Most of what people believe about how these tools learn, remember, and search is wrong in
  ways that matter for classroom use.

## What a language model actually does

A large language model is a system that has been trained to predict what word comes next,
across an enormous amount of text. That's the whole mechanism. Everything else, the
conversation, the essay, the lesson plan, is that prediction running over and over.

Be blunt about what that rules out. The model isn't looking anything up. It has no database
it consults and no notion of a source. When it
produces a citation, it's producing the sequence of words a citation tends to look like. That
sequence is sometimes a real paper and sometimes isn't, and the model has no way to tell the
difference, because from the inside there's no difference.

This is also why the output is so fluent. Fluency is what the training optimizes
for. Accuracy comes along for the ride when the training text happened to be accurate and
consistent, and it doesn't when the text was thin, contested, or absent.

## Where it's strong, where it fails

### Strong: you supply the content, it changes the form

Summarizing a document you paste in. Rewriting your paragraph at a sixth-grade reading
level. Turning your rubric into a student-facing checklist. Translating your worksheet.
Reformatting your notes into slides. Explaining your own text back to you in different
terms.

In all of these the substance is already in front of the model. It isn't being asked to
know anything, only to restate. That's the task the mechanism is good at, and it's most
of what a teacher needs.

### Weak: you ask it to supply the content

Facts it has to recall. Citations. Anything numeric. Recent events. Anything where being
almost right is the same as being wrong.

This is the failure that catches people. The model doesn't know when it doesn't know. It has no internal signal for the difference
between a well-supported answer and a fabricated one, so it delivers both in the same
confident register. A human expert hedges when they're unsure. This won't.

### The rule of thumb

Before you use one of these tools for something, ask where the content is coming from. If
it's coming from you and the tool is changing its shape, you're on solid ground. If it's
coming from the tool, you have to check it, and checking it often costs more than doing it
yourself would have.

That single question predicts most of what you'll experience in Sessions 4, 5 and 6.

## Common misconceptions

**"It searches the internet."** Usually not. Unless a tool explicitly says it's browsing or
retrieving, it's generating from training, and the training has a cutoff date.

**"It learns from our conversation."** Not in the way people mean. Some products have a
memory feature that saves notes about you, but a plain chat doesn't change the model.
Nothing your students type is teaching it.

**"It'll get the math right, it's a computer."** It's a language model, not a calculator.
Arithmetic is a sequence-prediction problem to it, and it approximates.

**"It can tell you whether something was AI-written."** It can't, and it will confidently
say yes or no when asked. More on this in Session 3.

**"It understands what it's saying."** Set this one aside rather than argue it. For
classroom purposes the question doesn't need answering, because the behavior is the same
either way, and the behavior is what you're planning around.
